title: Unification of Italy
competency: State the factors that helped Italian unification, appreciate the roles of its leaders and outline its process.

keywords.def: Joining separate states into one nation-state, as in Italy and Germany.
The existing state of affairs, kept unchanged.

Unity achieved by a government, its diplomats and its army, not by a popular uprising.
Fighting by small, mobile volunteer bands using surprise attacks.

en.text: Italian unification joined the states of the peninsula into one nation, from the Congress of Vienna (1815) to the Franco-Prussian War (1871). In 1852 Austria ruled Lombardy and Venetia and dominated Parma, Modena, Tuscany and Naples; the pope ruled the Papal States, guarded by a French garrison since 1849. Only Piedmont, under Victor Emmanuel II, was independent and constitutional, so it led. The obstacles were Austria's power and weak national feeling; Austria's isolation after the Crimean War (1853–56) and French–Austrian rivalry helped.

en.text: Camillo Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont from 1852 until his death in 1861, was the main architect of unification "from above". At Plombières in July 1858 he won Napoleon III's alliance against Austria. In April 1859 he provoked Austria into war; French and Piedmontese forces won at Magenta (4 June) and Solferino (24 June 1859), and Piedmont gained Lombardy, though Austria kept Venetia. Henri Dunant's experience at Solferino led to the Red Cross. In 1859 Romagna, Parma, Modena and Tuscany revolted and joined Piedmont.

ideas.name: Garibaldi and the completion of unity

en.text: In 1860 Sicily rose against Naples. Garibaldi led his Thousand Volunteers there on condition of unity under Victor Emmanuel, and took Naples on 7 September 1860, helped by his guerrilla skill and personality, mass support, and the demoralised Neapolitan army. After the fall of Gaeta, the first Italian parliament met at Turin on 18 February 1861 and Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of Italy on 17 March 1861. Italy gained Venetia through the Austro-Prussian War (1866) and seized Rome in September 1870, which became the capital.

notes.text: p.12: Crimean War printed "(1855–56)"; it lasted 1853–1856 (Piedmont joined in 1855). Taught as 1853–56.
p.12: Cavour "prime minister of Piedmont from 1852–62" is impossible (he died 6 June 1861). Taught as 1852–61 (out of office briefly 1859–60).
Spellings corrected: "Plombiere" → Plombières (July 1858); "Salferino" → Solferino (24 June 1859; Magenta 4 June 1859), also in Review I Q2.
p.14: 18 February 1861 is when the first Italian parliament met in Turin; Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of Italy on 17 March 1861. The lesson teaches both dates.

Activity 1.7 Q2 (Volturno): the text never mentions the Volturno or explains Cavour's decision. The practice item uses standard history and is marked added; teachers should supply the background (Volturno, 1 October 1860; Teano, 26 October 1860).
